questions.prompt: What is the core difference between a functional requirement and a nonfunctional requirement (NFR)?
options: An NFR only applies to Apex code, never to declarative automation
A functional requirement describes what the system does; an NFR describes how well it does it
A functional requirement is always more important to the business than an NFR
There is no real difference between the two terms
questions.explain: Functional requirements are testable pass/fail statements of what a system does. NFRs describe quality attributes — speed, availability, security, and similar — that determine how well the system performs those functions.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A is wrong because NFRs apply equally to declarative automation (Flow, validation rules) and Apex — nothing about the NFR/functional distinction is tool-specific.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder says a page "should load fast." What three components does this statement need before it becomes a real, testable performance NFR?
options: A budget, a deadline, and an executive sponsor
A governor limit, a sandbox, and a deployment pipeline
A metric, a numeric target, and a load condition
A security review, a compliance sign-off, and a test script
questions.explain: A real performance requirement names a metric (e.g., page load time), a numeric target (e.g., under 3 seconds), and the condition under which that target applies (e.g., for 95% of requests at 200 concurrent users). Without all three, the statement can't be tested.

questions.prompt: In the CIA triad as applied to a Salesforce security NFR, what does "confidentiality" mean?
options: The data is accurate and hasn't been tampered with
Authorized users can access the data whenever they legitimately need it
Only authorized people or systems can see the data
The organization has documented a legal basis before collecting the data
questions.explain: Confidentiality is the CIA triad property concerned specifically with who is allowed to see data, enforced through mechanisms like field-level security, sharing rules, and encryption.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes integrity, a separate CIA triad property about data accuracy, not about who can view the data.

questions.prompt: A report runs in two seconds against 50,000 records but takes two minutes against 50 million records, with no change to the report itself. What does this illustrate?
options: That scalability and performance are the same NFR measured at two different times
That performance and scalability are distinct NFRs — the system had good performance at a given volume but poor scalability as volume grew
That the report has a security NFR failure, not a performance issue
That Salesforce governor limits only apply to Apex, not to reports
questions.explain: Performance asks whether the system is fast enough right now. Scalability asks whether it stays fast enough as volume grows. This example shows good performance at the original volume but a scalability failure as data volume grew.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a property where performing the same operation more than once produces the same result as performing it once is called ________.
questions.explain: Idempotency is the reliability property that matters most for integrations, since network failures guarantee that operations will sometimes be retried, and a retried operation must not create a duplicate or corrupt the data.

questions.prompt: Match each maintainability or recoverability tool to what it actually does.
left: Source control and a deployment pipeline (Salesforce DX, sandboxes, CI/CD)
Field history tracking / Field Audit Trail
right: Preserves a record of a field's prior values, supporting recovery and audit after a bad data change
Turns configuration and code changes into a reviewable, versioned, auditable history instead of untracked production edits
Gives teams an environment to build and test changes without touching production
Provides automated, encrypted backups of standard/custom object data with a defined restore path
questions.explain: Source control and a deployment pipeline make changes reviewable and auditable. Sandboxes give a safe environment to build and test without touching production. Backup and Restore provides automated, encrypted backup and restore. Field history tracking preserves prior field values to support recovery and audit.

questions.prompt: Why does this course describe HIPAA as not being a certification that Salesforce (or any vendor) can be directly awarded?
options: Because HIPAA only applies to on-premises software, never cloud platforms
Because HIPAA was fully replaced by GDPR for all U.S. companies
Because HIPAA compliance is granted automatically once a vendor earns ISO 27001 certification

Because HIPAA is enforced through Business Associate Agreements and each covered entity's own compliance program, rather than a pass/fail audit of a platform — Salesforce instead supports HIPAA-relevant use cases through a HITRUST-audited report
questions.explain: HIPAA compliance is established through Business Associate Agreements and the covered entity's own program, not a certification a vendor earns outright. Salesforce supports HIPAA-relevant use cases via a HITRUST-audited report rather than claiming a direct 'HIPAA certification.'

questions.prompt: Why is walking a specific scenario like "50,000 new cases arrive in six hours after a product recall" through a proposed design an especially effective NFR elicitation technique?
options: Because it is the only elicitation technique that works for Salesforce projects
Because unusual, high-stakes situations are exactly the kind stakeholders wouldn't think to mention in the abstract, even though an NFR gap in exactly that scenario tends to be the most damaging
Because it eliminates the need to ever test the resulting NFR
Because it only surfaces compliance NFRs, never performance NFRs
questions.explain: Scenario walkthroughs surface requirements tied to unusual situations that rarely come up day-to-day and therefore rarely get mentioned unprompted — even though a gap in exactly that scenario is often where the real damage happens.

questions.prompt: What is the test this course gives for whether tracing an NFR to a design decision actually accomplished anything?
options: Whether the NFR document was approved at a governance checkpoint
Whether the NFR was written in the exact metric/target/condition format
Whether you can point to a specific design decision and say which NFR caused it to be made differently than the default, including an alternative you explicitly rejected
Whether the NFR is longer than a single sentence
questions.explain: A technically well-written NFR that never changes a design decision hasn't done its job. The real test is tracing a specific decision back to a specific NFR and a specific rejected alternative — if no alternative was rejected, the NFR likely didn't actually change anything.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of turning an NFR into a documented, traceable design decision in the correct order.
items: State the NFR in metric/target/condition form (or the equivalent for its category)
Identify the architectural implication — what the requirement rules out or demands
Make the specific design decision, naming what alternative was rejected and why
Record the decision in the NFR register or an architecture decision record, referencing the NFR's ID
questions.explain: The trace pattern runs from the stated requirement, to its architectural implication, to the specific decision (with a named rejected alternative), to a documented record that ties the decision back to the requirement's ID for future reference.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about testing approaches for different NFR categories.
options: Performance and scalability are tested through load testing: simulating the specified condition against a realistic environment and measuring the actual metric against the target
Reliability is tested through failure injection: deliberately causing the specified failure condition to verify the system's response actually works
Compliance is best tested purely with an automated script, with no need for a qualified human reviewer
Salesforce's Security Health Check fully substitutes for testing record-level and field-level access against an NFR's specific requirements
Maintainability is typically assessed through code/configuration review against stated conventions, since it's hard to test with a fully automated script
questions.explain: Load testing fits performance/scalability, and failure injection fits reliability. Compliance usually needs a qualified reviewer's judgment, not just an automated script, and Security Health Check is a useful first-pass org-wide check but does not substitute for directly testing record-level and field-level access against a specific NFR. Maintainability is generally assessed through review rather than an automated test.

questions.prompt: Why are compliance NFRs described as usually the least negotiable when they conflict with another NFR category?
options: Because compliance NFRs are always the cheapest and fastest to implement

Because compliance NFRs typically carry legal or contractual consequences the business has already accepted, so when they conflict with cost, timeline, or performance, it's usually those other factors that bend instead
Because compliance NFRs never actually conflict with any other NFR category in practice
Because Salesforce automatically enforces every compliance NFR without any implementation work
questions.explain: Because compliance obligations stem from already-accepted legal or contractual commitments, a genuine conflict usually resolves by bending the budget, timeline, or another NFR — not by quietly dropping the compliance requirement.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) measures the maximum acceptable amount of ________, measured as a time window.
questions.explain: RPO defines how much data loss, expressed as a span of time, is tolerable in a disaster. A tight RPO (e.g., 15 minutes) generally demands continuous or near-real-time replication rather than periodic backups.

questions.prompt: Why does this course warn against assuming a specific uptime percentage applies platform-wide across all Salesforce products and clouds?
options: Because Salesforce guarantees exactly 100% uptime in every contract, making the question moot

Because trust.salesforce.com is a transparency/status site publishing incident and performance information, not itself a universal contractual guarantee — some specific products carry their own numeric SLA in their own agreements, which should be verified against the current signed contract rather than assumed platform-wide
Because Salesforce has never published any uptime-related information anywhere
Because uptime commitments only ever apply to Government Cloud customers
questions.explain: trust.salesforce.com publishes status information, which is distinct from a contractually guaranteed percentage with a financial remedy. Any specific product's SLA should be checked against its own current agreement, not assumed to apply across the whole platform.

questions.prompt: In the high-volume service-org case study, why were performance, scalability, and reliability identified as the dominant NFR categories rather than compliance?
options: Because compliance NFRs never apply to Service Cloud implementations

Because this scenario's real risk is volume-driven — spike performance, transaction-volume scalability, and integration reliability during exactly those spikes — with no regulated data category forcing a compliance-heavy design
Because performance always outranks every other NFR category in every scenario, with no exceptions
Because the retailer had no customers during a product recall
questions.explain: Not every org needs the same NFR emphasis. This case study's finding is that the retailer's actual risk profile is dominated by volume-driven pressures, not a regulated-data compliance driver — which is the direct contrast with the financial-services case study.

questions.prompt: In the regulated financial-services case study, why do compliance, security, and recoverability dominate while performance and scalability are secondary?
options: Because Financial Services Cloud technically cannot support high transaction volume

Because this firm's data and transaction volumes never approach a scale that forces a difficult performance or scalability trade-off, while regulatory recordkeeping, data confidentiality, and loss scenarios define its real risk profile
Because compliance always outranks every other NFR category in every scenario, regardless of business context
Because the firm has no advisors handling client data
questions.explain: The same six-category framework, applied honestly to a different business, produces a different priority order: this firm's modest, steady volume means performance/scalability aren't the forcing function, while regulatory and confidentiality obligations are.

questions.prompt: Match each common NFR mistake to the specific fix or discipline that addresses it.
left: Writing an NFR with no metric, target, or condition
Treating a demo or pilot as proof an NFR is satisfied
Deciding a design without ever stating which NFR drove it
Pretending a genuine NFR conflict has no trade-off
right: Name the conflict explicitly and document which NFR bends, by how much, and who approved it
Write the requirement's trace — requirement, implication, decision, and rejected alternative
Force the requirement into metric, target, and condition before accepting it as finished
Test the actual stated condition (load, failure, audit) rather than whatever easy condition happens to be available
questions.explain: Each mistake has a specific discipline that closes it: vague statements need the metric/target/condition structure; demo-only validation needs testing against the actual stated condition; undocumented decisions need the requirement-implication-decision trace; and unacknowledged conflicts need the conflict to be named and the trade-off documented and approved.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an "evidence-based pass" on an NFR review checklist from a verbal-assurance pass?
options: An evidence-based pass requires executive sign-off only, with no technical detail
There is no real difference between the two — both are equally valid ways to mark a checklist item complete

An evidence-based pass is supported by documented proof — a specific test result, date, and measured number — that can be defended later or handed to the next architect, rather than just an assurance that something was done
An evidence-based pass only applies to the compliance NFR category
questions.explain: The review checklist contrasts a 'pass' based on a quick click-through feeling fast against a documented load test with a specific date, simulated volume, and measured percentile result — only the documented version can be defended later or verified by someone else.

questions.prompt: Why does an NFR register need an assigned owner and a defined trigger for revisiting it, rather than being written once at project kickoff?
options: Because Salesforce automatically deletes NFR registers older than one year
Because business requirements, regulations, and actual production volumes change over time, and a register that's never revisited goes stale exactly as fast as any other static document
Because registers must legally be rewritten from scratch every sprint
Because only compliance NFRs ever need to be revisited after launch
questions.explain: Conditions accurate at launch — a performance target, a regulatory assumption, a data-volume estimate — can become outdated as the business and its environment change, so the register needs an owner and a defined trigger (a major release, an annual review, a new regulation) to stay current and trusted.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of rehearsing an NFR defense for an architecture review board in the correct order.
items: State the design decision out loud, in one or two sentences, as if presenting it for the first time
Have a practice partner ask "why" at least three times, each time pushing on the weakest part of the previous answer
Answer each "why" using the trace structure: requirement, implication, decision, rejected alternative
Introduce a changed assumption and defend whether the same decision still holds, or explain specifically what would change
questions.explain: The rehearsal format runs from stating the decision, through repeated 'why' probing that mimics real board questioning, to answering in the trace structure, and finally stress-testing the reasoning against a changed assumption — checking understanding, not just a memorized number.
